column1: Annual Data by Plot and Treatment

column4: Workbook Annual Data gives the sunflower annual crop characteristics such as final canopy size, biomass, and yield by year, by plot and treatment;and seasonal water balance components.  Above Ground Biomass (AGB), Leaf Area Index (LAI), Harvest Index (HI), and 1000 seed mass were measured on plant samples collected at plant maturity.   Additional biomass data are reported in the Biomass workbook.  Maximum Canopy Cover and Intercepted Photosynthetically Active Radiation (IPAR) was measured periodically through the season (see CanopyCover workbook) and the maximum seasonal values are listed in this Workbook.  Seed Yield was measured at harvest on approximately 4 row x 20 m (60 m2) yield samples from the center of the plots.  Harvest samples involved collecting and threshing all heads to remove seed, measuring seed moisture content and correcting to 10% moisture content.  Seed oil content was measured on yield subsamples.  Treatment means are the average of 4 replicated plots of the same treatment.  Irrigation water applied included all irrigations applied through the season including sprinkler applied early season irrigation to promote germination and incorporate herbicides.  Irrigation water applied was measured by treatment and assumed equal to all plots within a treatment. Soil water content was measured in each plot 2 or 3  times per week by TDR (surface layer) and neutron moisture meter (30 cm increments to 200 cm.  Soil water storage is the volumetric SWC times the depth increment to the final root zone depth (135 cm) (see SoilWater workbook).  Initial (at planting) and final (132 days after planting) SW storage is extrapolated from the point in time measurements.  Positive values are SW added to storage over the season.  Seasonal Deep percolation (DP) (see Waterbalance workbook) is estimated water loss below the final root zone depth calculated by water balance.  Daily Precipitation is reported in the Weather and WaterBalance worksheets.  Actual Crop Evapotranspiration (ETa) was calculated by water balance (see Waterbalance workbook for daily values).  Crop Basal Evapotranspiration (ETab = ETa - soil evaporation) is based on estimated soil evaporation by FAO-56 methods.  Precipitation was assumed uniform across all plots; Irrigation was assumed uniform across all treatment plots; SW Storage change was the average of the 4 plots in each treatment.  Blank cells indicate missing data.

column1: Daily Water Balance Measured Data and Modeled Parameters by Year, Treatment, and Date (2008 - 2016)

column4: Daily values of crop status, water balance, soil water status, and derived evapotranspiration, by treatment, for the 2008 - 2016 LIRF sunflower deficit irrigation study. Data is ordered first by year, then treatment, then date.  Includes measured, calculated, and modeled values.  Blank cells indicate no data.  Daily Root Zone Depth was modeled to estimate the active root zone for crop water availability and soil water deficit (SWD) calculations.  Measured canopy cover was interpolated to daily values to estimate daily basal crop coefficients (Kcb).  Deep percolation was calculated by water balance.  Daily SWD was modeled to interpolate among measured SWD values and to calibrate Kcb values based on the water balance.  Daily SWD was used to model the crop stress coefficient (Ks).  Both tall and short crop reference evapotranspiration (ETr and ETo) were calculated from weather station data.  Daily basal evapotranspiration (ETab) values were calculated from the calibrated Kcb and Ks values.  Daily soil evaporation was modeled to convert daily ETab to a daily crop evapotranspiration (ETa).  Kcb values were also calculated directly from the water balance between soil water measurement dates (before irrigation) and converted to continuous trends with 15-day running averages.  Water balance modeling was based on FAO-56 techniques (Allen et al, 1998)

SWC was measured with a portable TDR probe (MiniTrase) with 15 cm probes from the surface to 15 cm.  SWC was measured with a neutron moisture meter (NMM; CPN-503 Hydroprobe, InstroTek, San Francisco, California) with the source centered at 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 200 cm. These data were subtracted from the field capacity for the plot (FC Worksheet) to calculate a plot soil water deficit, and deficits were averaged to determine treatment average deficit.

Field capacity was estimated by high seasonal values of SWC 24 hours after a large irrigation or precipitation event.  Initial FC values were from previous seasons on the same plot.  FC values were adjusted seasonally, as needed, such that the smallest soil water deficit (FC - SWC) values were near 0.

column1: Above-Ground Biomass by Plot and Treatment

column4: 5 plants in two sections (N and S) of the same row were sampled to determin above ground biomass (AGB).  Only one section was sampled in 2016 and other deviations are noted.    In 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2013 and 2016, only end-of-season (pre-harvest) samples were collected.  Above ground stalks were cut 4 cm above the surface, separated into leaves, heads, and stalks, dried at 65 deg C, and weighed.  Dried Seeds (kernal plus hull = cypsela) were separated from the heads and weighed.  Dried seed moistures were about 4% (by Dickey-john GAC mosture meter.)  Seed moisture was mathmatically adjusted to 10% to calculate seed yield.  Seed moisture was not adjusted to calculate AGB or harvest index.  Harvest index = dried seed mass/total dried above ground biomass.  Sample length (area) was only  measured in 2012, 2014, 2015, and 2016.  In other years, plot plant density (measured at harvest) was used to convert per plant biomass (g) to plot biomass (Kg ha-1).  Sample population was generally higher than plot population because sample areas were chosen with no plant skips.  Seed yield was yield only for the biomass sample.  Due to the small biomass sample size, plot yields should be used from the larger plot samples. Leaf Area Index was measured on the biomass sample either by measuring leaf area of the total sample and dividing by the total sample area, or measuring the leaf area of a subsample, then then drying and weighing the subsample to get the area per unit weight, then multiplying by the dry leaf weight of the total sample and dividing by the total sample area.

column1: Crop Canopy Ground Cover, IPAR, LAI, and Height

column4: This worksheet contains periodic measurements of sunflower canopy ground cover, Intercepted Photosynthetically Active Radiation (IPAR), Leaf Area Index (LAI), and plant height from 2008 - to - 2016 for the USDA-ARS LIRF Sunflower Water Use study.  Canopy Ground Cover was measured from nadir view digital RGB images taken 6 m above the ground (4 row x 4 m = 12 m2 area around the neutron access tube).  Canopy Cover Images were analyzed by differentiating the digital pixels between green plant canopy and background (soil, surface residue, and senesced leaves) with manually-trained image analysis software (DeJonge et al. 2024).  Canopy Cover was calculated as the ratio of green pixels to total pixels.  Because the Canopy Cover analysis methodology evolved over time, the images were re-analyzed in 2023 using a uniform process.  These results tended to exceed the original values.  If original images were not available, original analysis values were used but adjusted to re-analysis values using ratios of re-analysis to original values of similar data in the same year.  Adjusted original analysis data are shaded and the adjustment ratio shown in the embedded Note.  Blanks (shaded) cells indicate missing data.  Intercepted Photosynthetically Active radiation (IPAR) was measured within 30 min of solar noon on sunlit days with a light bar laid diagonally on the ground between two rows .  Leaf Area Index (LAI) was measured on subsamples of the biomass samples by calibrating the ratio of fresh leaf area (with a leaf area scanner) to leaf dry mass and multiplying the ratio by the leaf dry mass per plant and by the plant density.  Plant height was measured by a measurement rod to the top of the sunflower head.  Plant Height measurement dates varied from the row date and are noted in the first cell for each date.

column1: Length of root growth per minirhizotron viewing area by Plot and Treatment and Date

column4: This worksheet contains periodic measurements of sunflower root growth in the field in 2012 taken with a minirhizotron camera system.  Root populations were monitored through transparent plastic (cellulose acetate butyrate) root observation tubes (minirhizotrons), 183 cm long and 5.7 cm outside diameter in a column of 127 windows that were 18 mm × 13.5 mm.  Tubes were installed within one week of plant emergence at 30° from the vertical, 5-10 cm from the plant row half way between two plants and pointing into a plant’s root system by approximately 30° off of the row.  Images of roots visible in the windows were collected every two weeks through the growing season with a miniature video camera system (BTC-2 with I-CAP image capture; Bartz Technology Corp, Carpinteria, CA, USA).  Dates that individual roots were produced along with their lengths in every 5th window were recorded with RootFly 2.0 software (Clemson University, Clemson, SC, USA).

column1: Effective quantum yield (light-adapted chlorophyll fluorescence, (Fm' - Fs)/Fm') and Midday leaf water potential (?L)

column4: This worksheet contains periodic measurements of sunflower effective quantum yield (light-adapted chlorophyll fluorescence, Fm' - Fs)/Fm'), midday leaf water potential (LWP), and stomatal conductance (gs) collected in 2012 for the USDA-ARS LIRF Sunflower Water Use study.  Effective quantum yield was measured as a pulse amplitude modulated signal on one of the top 2 fully expanded leaves that were fully sunlit.  Measurements were taken with a fluorometer (OS5p; Opti-Sciences Inc, Hudson, New Hampshire, USA) halfway between the tip and the petiole as far in from the edge as the fluorometer could reach in a two-hour window prior to solar noon.  Intensity and gain settings were optimized to ensure a measurable signal with stable plateau following a saturating flash.  Midday leaf water potential (?L) was measured with a Scholander-type pressure chamber (Model 3005 Series Plant Water Status Console with a 18 cm long chamber, Soil Moisture Equipment Corp., Santa Barbara, CA, USA) within two hours past solar noon.  Fully expanded leaves in the sun were cut, put in a sealed plastic bag in a cooler until measurements were made.  Leaves were wrapped in a moistened cloth with the petiole fed through the lid of the chamber and re-cut immediately before pressurizing the chamber for measurements.
